collections.title: Hemoglobin and oxygen transport
collections.intro: Hemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to every tissue, and myoglobin stores it inside muscle. Comparing the deoxy (T state) and oxy (R state) structures shows how binding oxygen at one heme makes the other hemes grab oxygen more easily, the classic example of cooperativity. The collection also includes sickle cell hemoglobin and oxygen carriers from other organisms.

items.label: Human deoxyhemoglobin
items.note: The classic T-state structure from Max Perutz's group, used in countless textbooks.

items.label: Human oxyhemoglobin
items.note: Compare with 4HHB to see the T to R quaternary change.

items.label: Human carbonmonoxy hemoglobin
items.note: Carbon monoxide binds the same heme iron as oxygen, but far more tightly.

items.label: Deoxyhemoglobin bound to 2,3-DPG
items.note: 2,3-DPG (also called 2,3-BPG) stabilizes the T state and helps release oxygen in tissues.

items.label: T-state hemoglobin with oxygen at all four hemes
Sickle cell hemoglobin (deoxy HbS)
items.note: A single Glu to Val change in the beta chain lets deoxy HbS molecules stick together into fibers.

items.label: Sperm whale myoglobin
items.note: Myoglobin was the first protein whose 3D structure was solved, by John Kendrew's group.

items.label: Sperm whale oxymyoglobin at atomic resolution
Horseshoe crab hemocyanin, a copper-based oxygen carrier

collections.title: Insulin and hormones
collections.intro: Hormones are chemical messengers that travel through the blood and act on receptors in distant cells. Insulin, discovered in 1921, was one of the first proteins to be sequenced and crystallized, and its hexamers, analogs and receptor are shown here. The collection also covers growth hormone, leptin, erythropoietin, GLP-1 and the nuclear receptors that bind steroid hormones such as estrogen and testosterone.

items.label: Pig insulin hexamer with two zinc ions
items.note: Dorothy Hodgkin's group solved the first insulin structure in 1969.

items.label: Human insulin T6 hexamer at 1.0 Å
Insulin lispro, a fast-acting analog
items.note: Swapping two amino acids (ProB28 and LysB29) weakens the hexamer so the insulin acts faster.

items.label: Insulin bound to its receptor's binding site 1
Full-length insulin receptor bound to four insulins
Insulin receptor kinase domain with substrate peptide
Activated GLP-1 receptor bound to a G protein
items.note: GLP-1 receptor drugs such as semaglutide are used for diabetes and weight loss.

items.label: Human growth hormone bound to its receptor
Estrogen receptor with 4-hydroxytamoxifen
items.note: Tamoxifen blocks estrogen signaling in many breast cancers.

collections.title: SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19
collections.intro: Within months of the COVID-19 outbreak, scientists had solved structures of almost every SARS-CoV-2 protein. The spike protein binds the human ACE2 receptor and was the basis for the mRNA vaccines, while the main protease and RNA polymerase are targets of antiviral drugs such as nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid) and remdesivir. These structures show how structural biology guided the pandemic response.

items.label: Prefusion spike with one receptor-binding domain up
items.note: One of the first SARS-CoV-2 spike structures, released in February 2020.

items.label: Omicron spike bound to human ACE2
Spike protein encoded by the BNT162b2 vaccine
items.note: The protein that cells make from the Pfizer-BioNTech mRNA vaccine.

items.label: Receptor-binding domain bound to ACE2
items.note: Shows exactly where the virus grips the human receptor.

items.label: Receptor-binding domain with full-length ACE2 and B0AT1
Main protease with nirmatrelvir
items.note: Nirmatrelvir (PF-07321332) is the antiviral in Paxlovid.

items.label: RNA polymerase with RNA and remdesivir
Spike with the S309 antibody Fab
items.note: S309 is the parent antibody of the drug sotrovimab.

items.label: SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein (AlphaFold)
items.note: A predicted model of a viral protein, for comparison with the experimental spike structures.

collections.title: DNA and RNA
collections.intro: DNA stores genetic information in a double helix, and RNA copies, carries and even catalyzes with it. This collection starts with classic B-DNA, Z-DNA and RNA helices, then shows how proteins read DNA sequences, how DNA is packed into nucleosomes, and how polymerases copy it. It also includes folded RNAs such as transfer RNA, ribozymes and riboswitches.

items.label: B-DNA dodecamer (Dickerson dodecamer)
items.note: The first crystal structure of a full turn of B-DNA.

items.label: B-DNA dodecamer with bound cisplatin
items.note: Cisplatin is a cancer drug that attacks DNA.

items.label: Nucleosome core particle at 1.9 Å
items.note: DNA wrapped around eight histone proteins, the basic unit of chromatin.

items.label: Zif268 zinc fingers bound to DNA
Lambda repressor bound to operator DNA
Trp repressor bound to operator DNA
Lac repressor dimer bound to operator DNA
GCN4 leucine zipper bound to DNA
p53 tumor suppressor bound to DNA
GAL4 transcription factor bound to DNA
TATA-binding protein bound to a TATA box
TFIIB, TBP and TATA box ternary complex
HhaI DNA methyltransferase with DNA
items.note: This enzyme flips its target base out of the double helix.

items.label: DNase I, an enzyme that cuts DNA
RNA polymerase II
items.note: Part of the work recognized by the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Roger Kornberg).

items.label: Human topoisomerase I bound to DNA
Group I intron P4-P6 ribozyme domain

collections.title: Enzymes: how proteins speed up chemistry
collections.intro: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, often by millions of times, by holding their substrates in exactly the right position. These classic structures show active sites, catalytic triads, induced fit and large domain motions. Many of them, such as lysozyme, chymotrypsin and triosephosphate isomerase, are the standard examples in biochemistry courses.

items.label: Hen egg-white lysozyme
items.note: The first enzyme structure ever solved (David Phillips, 1965).

items.label: Triosephosphate isomerase
items.note: A nearly perfect enzyme, and the protein that gave the TIM barrel fold its name.

items.label: Yeast triosephosphate isomerase with an intermediate analog
Alpha-chymotrypsin
items.note: A serine protease with the classic Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad.

items.label: Adenylate kinase, closed form with inhibitor Ap5A
items.note: Compare with 4AKE to see the lids close over the substrates.

items.label: Human carbonic anhydrase II
items.note: One of the fastest enzymes known.

items.label: TEM-1 beta-lactamase
items.note: Destroys penicillin-type antibiotics, a major cause of antibiotic resistance.

items.label: Xylose isomerase
items.note: Used in industry to make high-fructose corn syrup.

items.label: Nitrogenase complex
items.note: Converts nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia.

collections.title: Antibodies and the immune system
collections.intro: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that recognize foreign molecules with great precision using the loops at the tips of their arms. This collection shows whole antibodies, antibody fragments bound to their targets, and therapeutic antibodies used against cancer and autoimmune disease. It also includes the MHC molecules and T-cell receptors that let the immune system spot infected cells.

items.label: Intact human IgG1 antibody b12 against HIV
Human IgG1 antibody with a hinge deletion
Human Fc fragment with protein A
IgG1 Fc bound to Fc gamma receptor III
IgE Fc bound to its high-affinity receptor
items.note: This interaction triggers allergic reactions.

items.label: IgM Fc with J chain and polymeric Ig receptor
Antibody Fab D1.3 bound to lysozyme
Antibody Fab HyHEL-10 bound to lysozyme
Camel single-domain antibody bound to lysozyme
items.note: Single-domain antibodies from camels and llamas are also called nanobodies.

items.label: VEGF bound to a neutralizing antibody Fab
HIV gp120 bound to antibody VRC01
Mouse MHC class I H-2Kb with a viral peptide
T-cell receptor bound to HLA-A2 and a viral peptide
T-cell receptor 2C bound to MHC H-2Kb

collections.title: Membrane proteins and transporters
collections.intro: Membrane proteins sit in the fatty lipid bilayer that surrounds every cell, where they move nutrients, pump ions, sense signals and let water through. They are hard to crystallize, so each of these structures was a major achievement. About a third of all human proteins, and a large share of drug targets, are membrane proteins.

items.label: Aquaporin-1 water channel
items.note: Aquaporins were recognized by the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Peter Agre).

items.label: SERCA calcium pump with two calcium ions
Human P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) with taxol
items.note: P-glycoprotein pumps drugs out of cells and can make tumors resistant to chemotherapy.

items.label: Human CFTR chloride channel
items.note: Mutations in CFTR cause cystic fibrosis.

items.label: LeuT, a bacterial neurotransmitter transporter homolog

collections.title: AlphaFold highlights
collections.intro: AlphaFold is an AI system that predicts a protein's 3D structure from its amino acid sequence, and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. These predicted models cover famous human proteins, including several that are hard to study experimentally because they are large, flexible or embedded in membranes. Color by confidence (pLDDT) to see which parts of each model are reliable and which are likely disordered.

items.label: p53 tumor suppressor
items.note: The most frequently mutated gene in human cancer.

items.label: BRCA1 breast cancer protein
items.note: Large parts of BRCA1 are predicted to be disordered.

collections.title: Photosynthesis
collections.intro: Photosynthesis turns sunlight into chemical energy and releases the oxygen we breathe. Light-harvesting complexes collect photons and pass the energy to reaction centers, where it drives electron transfer across a membrane. Photosystem II splits water, and the enzyme Rubisco then fixes carbon dioxide into sugar.

items.label: Bacterial photosynthetic reaction center
items.note: The first membrane protein structure solved at atomic detail, recognized by the 1988 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

items.label: Light-harvesting complex LH2 from a purple bacterium
Photosystem II at 1.9 Å
items.note: Revealed the Mn4CaO5 cluster that splits water into oxygen.

items.label: Activated spinach Rubisco
items.note: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide and is probably the most abundant protein on Earth.

collections.title: Motor proteins and the cytoskeleton
collections.intro: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments that gives cells their shape and acts as tracks for transport. Motor proteins such as myosin, kinesin and dynein burn ATP to walk along these tracks, contracting muscles and carrying cargo. This collection shows actin, tubulin and the motors that move along them.

items.label: Actin bound to DNase I
items.note: The first atomic structure of actin, solved as a complex with DNase I.

items.label: Tubulin with taxol
items.note: The cancer drug taxol (paclitaxel) stabilizes microtubules.

items.label: Chicken muscle myosin subfragment-1 (the motor head)
Dictyostelium myosin motor domain with ADP
Scallop myosin S1 in the pre-power stroke state

collections.title: Ion channels
collections.intro: Ion channels are gated pores that let specific ions such as potassium, sodium or calcium cross the cell membrane. They generate nerve impulses, heartbeats and muscle contraction, and sense heat, touch and chemical signals. The KcsA potassium channel structure explained for the first time how a channel can be both fast and highly selective.

items.label: KcsA potassium channel
items.note: Recognized by the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Roderick MacKinnon).

items.label: KcsA potassium channel in high potassium
Human Nav1.2 sodium channel with a cone snail toxin
GLIC, a bacterial pentameric ligand-gated channel
TRPV1 heat and capsaicin receptor
items.note: TRPV1 senses heat and the spicy compound in chili peppers (2021 Nobel Prize in Medicine).

collections.title: GPCRs and cell signaling
collections.intro: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the largest family of membrane receptors and the targets of about a third of approved drugs. They detect light, smells, hormones and neurotransmitters, then switch on G proteins inside the cell. The beta-2 adrenergic receptor structures were recognized by the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

items.label: Bovine rhodopsin
items.note: The first GPCR structure, solved in 2000.

items.label: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor bound to Gs protein
Adenosine A2A receptor with antagonist ZM241385
Mouse mu-opioid receptor with an antagonist
Active mouse mu-opioid receptor with agonist BU72
Mouse mu-opioid receptor bound to Gi protein
Active M2 muscarinic receptor with iperoxo
CCR5 chemokine receptor with maraviroc
items.note: CCR5 is a co-receptor HIV uses to enter cells.

items.label: Angiotensin II type 1 receptor with olmesartan
Smoothened receptor with an anticancer drug
GLP-1 receptor bound to Gs protein
GABA-B receptor in the active state

collections.title: Kinases and cancer drug targets
collections.intro: Protein kinases switch other proteins on and off by adding phosphate groups, and when they are stuck in the on position they can drive cancer. Imatinib (Gleevec), which blocks the BCR-ABL kinase in leukemia, showed that drugs designed against a specific kinase can work. This collection shows kinases with the drugs that target them, along with other famous cancer targets such as Ras, p53, MDM2, BCL-2 and PARP.

items.label: Protein kinase A with ATP and a peptide inhibitor
items.note: PKA was the first protein kinase structure solved and became the model for the whole family.

items.label: Cyclin A bound to cyclin-dependent kinase 2
PI3K alpha lipid kinase with an inhibitor
H-Ras bound to a GTP analog
KRas G12C with sotorasib (AMG 510)
items.note: Sotorasib was the first approved drug to target a mutant Ras protein.

items.label: MDM2 bound to a p53 peptide

collections.title: Viruses
collections.intro: Viruses are tiny packages of genetic material wrapped in a protein shell, often with a membrane studded with glycoproteins. Many viral capsids are built from repeated copies of a few proteins arranged with beautiful icosahedral symmetry. This collection covers capsids and the surface proteins of influenza, HIV, Ebola, dengue, Zika, RSV and other viruses, many of which are vaccine and drug targets.

items.label: Tobacco mosaic virus
items.note: The first virus ever discovered.

items.label: Human papillomavirus 16 L1 capsid protein
items.note: L1 is the protein used in HPV vaccines.

items.label: HIV-1 gp120 bound to CD4 and an antibody
Ebola virus glycoprotein with a survivor's antibody
RSV fusion protein, prefusion form
items.note: Stabilizing this prefusion shape led to the first RSV vaccines.

collections.title: The ribosome and protein synthesis
collections.intro: The ribosome is the molecular machine that reads messenger RNA and joins amino acids into proteins. It is made mostly of RNA, and its core chemistry is carried out by RNA rather than protein. Ribosome structures were recognized by the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and explain how many antibiotics work. Note that full ribosomes are very large and may take a while to load.

items.label: 30S subunit with streptomycin, spectinomycin and paromomycin
50S subunit with the antibiotic carbomycin A
Isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase with tRNA and mupirocin

collections.title: CRISPR and genome editing
collections.intro: CRISPR systems began as a bacterial immune defense against viruses and became a precise tool for editing genes, recognized by the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Cas9 uses a guide RNA to find a matching DNA sequence next to a short PAM motif and then cuts both strands. The collection also covers Cas12, Cas13, base editors and older programmable tools such as TALEs and zinc fingers.

items.label: Cas9 with guide RNA and target DNA
Cas9 bound to a PAM-containing target
Cas9 R-loop complex primed for DNA cleavage
Staphylococcus aureus Cas9 with sgRNA and DNA
ABE8e adenine base editor
items.note: A base editor changes a single DNA letter without cutting both strands.

items.label: Cas12a (Cpf1) with crRNA and target DNA
Cas12b (C2c1) with sgRNA and target DNA
Cas13a with CRISPR RNA
items.note: Cas13 targets RNA instead of DNA and is used in diagnostic tests.

items.label: Cas13a with crRNA and target RNA
Cascade surveillance complex bound to DNA
TAL effector PthXo1 bound to DNA
Zif268 zinc fingers bound to DNA

collections.title: Fluorescent and glowing proteins
collections.intro: Green fluorescent protein (GFP) from a jellyfish forms its own light-emitting chromophore inside a barrel of beta strands, which lets scientists tag and watch proteins in living cells. Its discovery and development won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Engineered variants and proteins from corals now cover every color, and some can be switched on and off with light.

items.label: GFP bound to an anti-GFP nanobody

collections.title: Neurotransmission and the synapse
collections.intro: Nerve cells talk to each other at synapses by releasing neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, serotonin and dopamine. Receptors on the next cell open ion channels or trigger signaling, and transporters and enzymes then clear the signal. Many medicines, toxins and drugs of abuse act on the proteins shown here.

items.label: Human acetylcholinesterase with donepezil
items.note: Donepezil is used to treat symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.

items.label: GABA-B receptor in the active state
Fruit fly dopamine transporter with nortriptyline
SNARE complex for synaptic vesicle fusion
Botulinum neurotoxin type A
items.note: Botox works by cutting a SNARE protein so vesicles cannot fuse.

collections.title: Blood clotting
collections.intro: When a blood vessel is damaged, a cascade of proteases activates one another and finally turns soluble fibrinogen into a fibrin mesh that seals the wound. Thrombin and factor Xa sit at the center of this cascade and are the targets of modern anticoagulants such as apixaban and rivaroxaban. Clot-busting enzymes such as tissue plasminogen activator later break the clot down.

items.label: Thrombin bound to hirudin
items.note: Hirudin is the anticoagulant in leech saliva.

items.label: Factor VIIa bound to tissue factor
Coagulation factor VIII
items.note: Missing or faulty factor VIII causes hemophilia A.

items.label: Von Willebrand factor A1 domain bound to platelet GPIb alpha
Plasmin catalytic domain bound to streptokinase
Human VKOR with warfarin
items.note: Warfarin blocks the vitamin K recycling needed to make clotting factors.

collections.title: Drugs bound to their targets
collections.intro: Seeing exactly how a drug sits in its target's binding pocket is the heart of structure-based drug design. The HIV protease inhibitors of the 1990s were among the first big successes of this approach. This collection pairs well-known medicines, from aspirin and statins to antivirals, with the proteins they block.

items.label: HIV-1 protease with a cyclic urea inhibitor
Prostaglandin H2 synthase (COX-1) inactivated by aspirin
HMG-CoA reductase with atorvastatin
items.note: Statins lower cholesterol by blocking this enzyme.

collections.title: Classic small proteins for teaching
collections.intro: Small, well-behaved proteins are ideal for learning how to read a structure: they load instantly and every helix and strand is easy to follow. Many of these, such as crambin, ubiquitin, BPTI and lysozyme, have been used for decades to test methods in crystallography, NMR, protein folding and computer simulation. Start here if you are new to molecular structures.

items.label: Crambin
items.note: A tiny plant protein of 46 residues that forms exceptionally well-ordered crystals.

items.label: Ubiquitin
items.note: The small tag that marks proteins for destruction by the proteasome.

items.label: Trp-cage miniprotein
items.note: Only 20 residues, a favorite test case for protein folding simulations.

items.label: Calmodulin wrapped around a target peptide
Streptavidin bound to biotin
items.note: One of the strongest non-covalent interactions known.

items.label: Top7, a computer-designed protein with a new fold

collections.title: Metabolism and cellular energy
collections.intro: Cells break down glucose step by step to capture its energy as ATP. Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate, the citric acid cycle oxidizes the fragments, and the respiratory chain in mitochondria uses the electrons to pump protons. ATP synthase, a rotary motor, then uses that proton flow to make ATP.

items.label: F1-ATPase, the catalytic head of ATP synthase
items.note: Recognized by the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (John Walker).

items.label: Mammalian ATP synthase tetramer with inhibitor IF1

collections.title: Protein folding, misfolding and amyloid
collections.intro: Proteins must fold into the right shape to work, and cells use chaperones such as GroEL and Hsp90 to help, and the proteasome to destroy proteins that fail. When folding goes wrong, some proteins stack into long amyloid fibrils. Fibrils of amyloid-beta, tau and alpha-synuclein are hallmarks of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, and misfolded prion proteins cause mad cow disease.

items.label: GroEL-GroES chaperonin complex
items.note: A folding chamber that gives a protein a protected space to fold.

items.label: Hsp90 chaperone in a closed state
HET-s prion in its amyloid form
Tau paired helical filament from Alzheimer's disease brain
Tau filament from chronic traumatic encephalopathy
Human transthyretin
items.note: Mutant transthyretin can form amyloid deposits in the heart and nerves.

collections.title: Toxins and how they work
collections.intro: Bacteria and plants make some of the most potent poisons known, and their structures reveal how they get into cells and what they attack. Many toxins have two parts: one that binds and enters the cell, and one that carries out the damage. Some, such as botulinum toxin, are also used as medicines.

items.label: Cholera toxin B pentamer bound to the GM1 sugar
